title: I built a procedural noir detective game where every case is a new murder.
author: denzelgamedev
selftext:
**Angled Watch** is a single-player 3D isometric detective game. Every case procedurally generates a fresh murder, a cast of look-alike suspects, and one killer who lies in every statement. You observe, tail suspects, catch the contradiction, and make **one** arrest. No two cases are the same.

**Where AI came in:** the 5 background music tracks are Suno (Pro license). Everything else is 100% procedural art (no downloaded models/textures/icons), the case generator, the noir render pipeline, all vanilla JS + Three.js, no engine.

**The hard part** was fairness: the generator has to guarantee every case is *solvable by observation alone* and that the killer is never findable by luck. That took a whole test suite of "solver bots" that try to cheat the case.

Playable free in-browser: [https://denzelgamedev.itch.io/angledwatch](https://denzelgamedev.itch.io/angledwatch)

Looking forward for your feedback!

comments.author: denzelgamedev
comments.body: For those who have tried, what do you think about the difficulty? Did I made it too easy? Is the interface tutorial confusing? Let me know your thoughts!

replies.author: promptling
replies.body: That one arrest constraint makes difficulty interesting: success rate alone won’t show whether players understood the contradiction or simply guessed. I’d ask players to explain their evidence before arresting, then compare confidence with correctness. I’m building [Patchloop](https://patchloop.io/) as a home for agentically built games and structured feedback loops; Angled Watch feels like a strong fit for repeated difficulty and tutorial tests.

replies.author: denzelgamedev
replies.body: That's an interesting suggestion and it left me reflecting for quite a lot of time (hence why I took so long to reply). If the suspect they are accusing meets the characteristics that the murder had, why would they need to explain their accusation? I see that you're using luck as an argument but that's already punishable in the game and in the later cases the tips get harder... Well, certainly something to think about and I thank you for that. Also it's great to see a platform that helps people refine their game since feedback is something very valuable and rare in the game dev area. Have a good one!

replies.author: denzelgamedev
replies.body: Sorry that you had to see the game in this state and thank you for testing out the game, I'll be seeing what I can do about this. If possible could you tell me your device model?

replies.author: denzelgamedev
replies.body: From what I understood, the game encoded its paper textures as PNG, and the S22 Ultra's driver corrupts canvas PNG encoding. That's what caused the stripes, I think. I switched them to JPEG and updated the build on itch, so if you give it another try in the future I'd love to know how it went. Sorry about that, and thanks for flagging it!
